passage: Before posting the photo from Saturday's trek, I tried three filters. I made the sky bluer and cropped out the muddy trousers. I wrote the caption 'Living my best life.' That was true, but it wasn't the whole truth, because I'd also slipped twice and been grumpy for an hour, and nobody would see it. I said this to Sudha, who laughed and said, "Everyone's feed is curated, Mohit. That's why mine looks calm too." I thought about that and posted it. But I asked Sudha before I put up the group shot she was in. She said yes to that one and no to the one where she was blinking. Now I try to remember that a post is a selected slice.

qa.q: How many filters did Mohit try on the trek photo?
qa.a: Mohit tried three filters.

qa.q: Why did Mohit feel that the caption was true but not the whole truth?
qa.a: Mohit felt the caption showed only the happy part and hid the two slips and the grumpy hour. Mohit realised what people see is chosen.

qa.q: What did Mohit do that showed care for a friend's image?
qa.a: Mohit asked Sudha before posting the group photo and accepted her no to the picture where she was blinking.

qa.q: How might a viewer who sees only the post feel about their own life?
qa.a: They might feel their day is duller or harder than others', not knowing it is curated.

grounding: A teen curates photos and captions for self-presentation, knows posts are a slice, and shares others' images with consent.

passage: Counselling note, Monday. Raghav came in after a classmate told him off for posting a class photo in which she was making a funny face. Raghav said she'd laughed at the time, so he thought it was fine. She hadn't said yes, and she has now asked him to remove it. He also mentioned that his own feed looks like everyone has amazing weekends, and that he sometimes feels bad comparing. We talked about how people choose the best photos and filters, and how other people's pictures need their permission. He agreed to take the photo down and ask before posting in future. I told him he can talk to me any time. Vidya, counsellor.

qa.q: What did Raghav's friend tell him off for?
qa.a: She told him off for posting a class photo in which she was making a funny face.

qa.q: What was Raghav thinking and feeling when he posted the photo?
qa.a: He felt at ease about it because she had laughed at the time. He had not asked her, so he had not checked what she felt.

qa.q: What steps did Raghav agree to?
qa.a: Take the photo down and ask before posting anyone's image in future.

qa.q: How might Raghav's friend have felt seeing the photo online?
qa.a: She may have felt embarrassed and exposed, since the picture went out without her say.

grounding: A teen curates a self-image and learns personal images should be shared only with consent.

passage:
Sunday
Scrolled through Pranav's holiday photos again. Beach sunset. Mango ice cream. His whole family laughing on a boat. Perfect filters. And I was stuck at home with fever all week.
I'll be honest, diary: I felt resentful. Why does he get a perfect life?
Then today at the library he said, "That trip was the worst. My parents fought the whole time. The boat photo was the only five minutes they were smiling."
I didn't know what to say. I just said, "I'm sorry."
It made me think about my own posts. I only post when my hair's good and the light's nice. Nobody sees me with fever and a tissue box.
So I posted a photo of me today, blanket and all. Caption: "real life 🤒." Then I asked Mehr before posting the one with her in it too.
- Zeenat

qa.q: What did Pranav say about the boat photo?
qa.a: He said the boat photo was the only five minutes they were smiling.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling when scrolling through Pranav's photos?
qa.a: Zeenat felt resentful and a bit envious, comparing a week of fever to what looked like his perfect holiday.

qa.q: What changed in how Zeenat chooses what to post?
qa.a: Zeenat posted an honest, unfiltered photo and asked Mehr's permission before sharing one with Mehr in it.

qa.q: How might Pranav feel seeing people envy his holiday posts?
qa.a: He might feel lonely or strange, since the posts hide how hard the trip really was.

grounding: The diary shows posted images as curated self-presentation that hides the full picture, and a teen choosing honesty and consent.

passage:
In the small town of Kotdwar, there was exactly one café with fairy lights, and Sharmila had posted from it eleven times. Always the same table, the same angle, the cold coffee in the frame, a caption like "city vibes ✨."
When her cousin Simran visited from her Delhi hostel, Sharmila took her there proudly.
Simran laughed. "So this is the famous place! You make it look like Paris."
Sharmila went red. "Everyone here posts like that. You post such amazing stuff from Delhi."
Simran was quiet. "I post the one night we went out. I don't post the forty nights I ate alone in my room."
Sharmila looked at her. "Seriously?"
"Seriously. Everyone's feed is a highlight reel."
They took a photo together, blurry, laughing, the tea spilled. Sharmila almost filtered it. Instead she asked, "Can I post this one? As is?"
"As is," Simran said.

qa.q: How many times had Sharmila posted from the café?
qa.a: Sharmila had posted from it eleven times.

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling when Simran joked about Paris?
qa.a: Sharmila felt embarrassed and exposed, going red, since her curated posts made the small café look grand.

qa.q: What choice did Sharmila make at the end, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She asked Simran's consent to post an unfiltered photo, showing honesty and care about sharing someone else's image.

qa.q: What is it like for Simran behind her Delhi posts?
qa.a: Simran seems lonely at the hostel, eating alone on most nights, which her posts never show.

grounding: The scene shows two teens discovering that curated posts hide the full picture of their lives, and sharing a photo with consent.

passage: Everyone in their Stockholm class agreed Emeka had the best feed: a sunset from the ferry, a perfect cinnamon bun, basketball mid-air. Ulla scrolled it on the bus home and felt a small hard knot in her chest. Her own weekend had been laundry and a fight with her brother. On Monday she said, a bit sharply, "Must be nice, living in a postcard." Emeka laughed, then stopped. "That sunset? I took forty photos and posted one. I was only on the ferry because my dad's shift moved and I had to pick up my sister. I was freezing." Ulla blinked. Then Emeka added, "Also, I posted the one from the class trip where your eyes are half closed. Sorry, I didn't ask. Want me to take it down?" "Yes, please," Ulla said. He deleted it while she watched, and they picked a better one together, which he posted only after she nodded.

qa.q: How many sunset photos did Emeka take?
qa.a: Emeka took forty photos and posted one.

qa.q: What was Ulla feeling as she scrolled Emeka's feed on the bus?
qa.a: Ulla felt a hard knot of resentment and envy, comparing a weekend of laundry and a fight with postcard-like photos; tiredness may also have made the gap feel bigger.

qa.q: What did Emeka do well?
qa.a: Emeka was honest that the sunset was one shot of forty and told the real story, and asked before reposting Ulla's picture, posting only after she nodded.

qa.q: What was it like for Emeka to hear 'living in a postcard'?
qa.a: It probably stung a little, since the real day was freezing and full of chores, and it also reminded Emeka that he hadn't asked about Ulla's photo.

grounding: It shows a teenager curating photos to present a polished self, a peer's resentment at the comparison, and asking consent before sharing someone else's image.
